title: Intermittent burning upper abdominal pain in a 45-year-old accountant
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 45-year-old man with 3 weeks of intermittent burning epigastric pain that comes after large meals and wakes him at night. He takes ibuprofen most days, smokes, is stressed at work and is worried about his heart. The candidate then interprets his ECG, blood tests and gastroscopy with biopsy, recognises a Helicobacter pylori duodenal ulcer with an NSAID contribution, and plans eradication therapy, NSAID withdrawal, confirmation of eradication and safety netting.
focus: Dyspepsia in general practice: ALARM features, peptic ulcer risk factors, and managing an H. pylori ulcer
stem: You are a GP in a metropolitan general practice. John Peters, a 45-year-old accountant, has come in because he has been having intermittent pain in his upper abdomen.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Peters and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Mr Peters' ECG, his blood test results and his gastroscopy and biopsy report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are John Peters, a 45-year-old accountant. You are polite but a bit stressed and tired, and you are quietly worried this might be your heart. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've been getting this burning pain up here in my upper tummy on and off for a few weeks." (point to the top of your abdomen, just below the breastbone)

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: upper tummy, in the middle. It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Started about 3 weeks ago and comes and goes.
  • It sometimes comes on 2 to 3 hours after a big meal. Each episode lasts 30 to 60 minutes.
  • It has woken you from sleep a few times.
  • It is a burning pain, about 3 to 4 out of 10.
  • It is linked to meals. Only if asked what makes it worse: spicy food.
  • Mylanta sometimes helps; usually it settles on its own.

Other symptoms (only if asked): your appetite is a bit down and you feel bloated.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Trouble swallowing, or pain when swallowing.
  • Weight loss, fevers, night sweats.
  • Tiredness, breathlessness, dizziness or looking pale.
  • Vomiting, vomiting blood or anything like coffee grounds.
  • Diarrhoea, blood in your poo, or black tarry poo. Your bowels are normal and you are passing wind.
  • Chest pain or tightness on exertion, pain going to your arm or jaw, sweating, breathlessness or palpitations with the pain.
  • A sudden tearing pain going through to your back.
  • Burning rising into your chest, food or sour fluid coming back into your mouth, or pain worse lying flat.
  • Pain on the right side under the ribs or going to your shoulder, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or pale poo.
  • Severe pain going through to the back, or a swollen tummy.
  • Pain in your side or loin, or burning or blood when passing urine.
  • Anyone around you with gastro.

Past medical history: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes controlled with diet, and osteoarthritis in your left knee. Only if asked about your weight: "The nurse said my BMI was 27." No operations. No recent travel. Immunisations up to date.

Medications:

  • Perindopril 2.5 mg daily.
  • Atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
  • Mylanta when needed.
  • Ibuprofen (Nurofen) for your knee: you take it most days and have done for over 10 years. You buy it at the supermarket.
  • No acid tablets (no PPI) and nothing else.

Allergies: peanuts (you vomit). No medicine allergies.

Family history:

  • Mother: "She had tummy ulcers that needed some sort of scope."
  • Father: heart attack at 60.
  • No one in the family has had stomach or bowel cancer.

Social history:

  • Smoke 10 cigarettes a day, for 15 years.
  • Alcohol: 1 to 2 standard drinks, once a week.
  • Accountant. Work has been very stressful: some colleagues were let go, your workload is bigger and you are worried about your own job.
  • No exercise. You enjoy spicy and fatty food.
  • Live with your wife and your cat. You feel well supported.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I'm not really sure what it is."
  • Concern: "I'm worried it might be my heart." If asked why: "My father had a heart attack when he was 60."
  • Expectation: "I just want to know what's going on!"

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Could this be my heart, doc?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: well, comfortable, not pale or jaundiced. Weight 85 kg, height 177 cm, BMI 27.
  • Observations: HR 72 regular, BP 136/84 (right and left arm similar), RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C, capillary BGL 6.8 mmol/L.
  • Hands and face: no clubbing, koilonychia or palmar pallor. Conjunctivae pink. No scleral icterus.
  • Neck: no supraclavicular (Virchow's) or cervical lymph nodes.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Peripheral pulses present and equal, no radio-radial delay.
  • Respiratory: chest clear.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Soft and non-tender, including the epigastrium; no guarding. Murphy's sign negative. No masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, no pulsatile mass. Bowel sounds normal. Renal angles not tender.
  • Rectal examination (if offered, with a chaperone): brown stool on the glove, no melaena or blood.
  • Left knee (if examined): bony crepitus, no effusion, full range of movement.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms John's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language, acknowledges his work stress and takes his worry about his heart seriously without dismissing it.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site, character and severity: central upper abdomen, no radiation, burning, 3 to 4/10.
Onset and timing: intermittent over 3 weeks, episodes of 30 to 60 minutes, 2 to 3 hours after large meals, waking him from sleep.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with spicy food; sometimes eased by antacids, usually settles by itself.

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms: mild loss of appetite and bloating.
Screens for ALARM symptoms:

kids.x: Weight loss or constitutional symptoms, and symptoms of anaemia (tiredness, breathlessness, dizziness).
Vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools or blood in the stool.

check.x: Screens for cardiac and aortic causes: exertional chest pain, radiation to the arm or jaw, sweating, breathlessness or palpitations, and sudden tearing pain to the back.

Asks questions that rule out other causes: reflux (heartburn, regurgitation, sour taste, worse lying flat); biliary, liver and pancreatic disease (right upper quadrant pain after fatty food, radiation to the shoulder or back, fever, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools); obstruction or gastroenteritis (vomiting, distension, bowel habit, sick contacts); renal colic (loin pain, urinary symptoms).
check.d: Award for a reasonable systems review covering at least three of these groups.

check.x: Asks about peptic ulcer risk factors:

kids.x: NSAID use: ibuprofen most days for over 10 years for his left knee.
Smoking (10 a day for 15 years) and alcohol (1 to 2 standard drinks once a week); notes work stress and spicy food as aggravating factors rather than causes.

check.x: Takes the past medical history: hypertension, high cholesterol, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, left knee osteoarthritis; no surgery or travel.
Takes a medication and allergy history: perindopril 2.5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, Mylanta as needed, no PPI; peanut allergy (vomiting) and no medicine allergies.
Takes a family history: mother had ulcers needing a scope, father had a heart attack at 60, no family history of stomach or bowel cancer.
Takes a social history: accountant with job stress after colleagues were let go, lives with his wife and cat, no exercise, enjoys spicy and fatty food, well supported.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, worried about his heart because of his father, wants to know what is going on.
Examination
Asks for vital signs, weight and BMI, and notes the vital signs are normal and the BMI of 27 is in the overweight range.
Looks for signs of anaemia, bleeding or malignancy: conjunctival and palmar pallor, koilonychia, jaundice and the left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node.
Examines the abdomen: inspection, palpation of all regions including the epigastrium (soft, non-tender, no guarding or masses), liver and spleen, Murphy's sign, a pulsatile mass, and bowel sounds.
Listens to the heart and chest and checks the peripheral pulses.
Offers a rectal examination with a chaperone to look for melaena, or states it is indicated if bleeding is suspected.
Summarises the examination: no alarm signs, normal apart from a BMI of 27.
Interpretation
Interprets the ECG: sinus rhythm at 72, normal axis and intervals, no ST or T wave changes; reassuring, but a normal resting ECG does not exclude coronary disease in a man with his risk factors.

Interprets the bloods: normal haemoglobin and MCV (no anaemia to suggest bleeding or malignancy), normal LFTs and lipase (against biliary disease, hepatitis and pancreatitis), and normal renal function.
Interprets the gastroscopy: an 8 mm clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer with no stigmata of recent bleeding, mild antral gastritis, and a normal oesophagus with no gastric ulcer or mass.
Interprets the biopsies: positive rapid urease test and H. pylori on histology with chronic active gastritis; no intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia or malignancy.
States the diagnosis as peptic ulcer disease (a duodenal ulcer) caused by H. pylori with long-term NSAID use contributing, justified by the pain pattern and the results.
Gives at least three differentials with a feature for or against each (for example GORD, functional dyspepsia, biliary colic, cardiac ischaemia, gastric cancer).
Management
Explains the diagnosis in plain words and answers his question about his heart: the normal ECG and the link to meals point to the ulcer, but a normal ECG does not rule out heart disease.
Prescribes H. pylori eradication therapy:

kids.x: Triple therapy: a PPI (for example esomeprazole 20 mg) plus amoxicillin 1 g plus clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily, for 14 days.
kids.d: Accept any PPI at the eTG eradication dose (e.g. esomeprazole 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg or rabeprazole 20 mg twice daily). Duration must be 14 days.

kids.x: Confirms there is no penicillin allergy before giving amoxicillin (his peanut allergy is not a contraindication).
Explains the need to finish the course and the common side effects (diarrhoea, taste disturbance), and withholds atorvastatin during the clarithromycin course because of the interaction.
kids.d: Award the interaction if the candidate checks it and acts on it.

check.x: Stops ibuprofen and offers alternatives for his knee (paracetamol, a topical NSAID, exercise and weight loss); if an oral NSAID is ever essential, gives it with a PPI.
Continues the PPI once daily for about 4 more weeks after the antibiotics to heal the ulcer (NSAID-associated), then stops it at least 2 weeks before the urea breath test; Mylanta as needed.
Plans to confirm eradication with a urea breath test at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics finish, with the PPI stopped for 2 weeks before the test.
Offers smoking cessation support (brief advice, Quitline, pharmacotherapy) because smoking delays ulcer healing.
Safety netting
Tells him to call 000 or go to the ED if he vomits blood or coffee-ground material, passes black tarry or bloody stools, feels faint or collapses, or gets sudden severe abdominal pain.

Tells him to call 000 for chest pain or tightness that is severe, getting worse or lasting more than 10 minutes, or comes with sweating, breathlessness or nausea; and to see the GP the same day if he gets chest tightness on exertion that settles with rest.
Tells him to see his GP sooner if the pain does not settle on treatment, or if he develops trouble swallowing, weight loss or persistent vomiting.
Arranges follow-up: GP review after the course (symptoms, side effects, restarting atorvastatin, knee pain plan), books the urea breath test, and arranges a cardiovascular risk assessment.

part2.lead: John had an ECG and blood tests at the practice on the day you first saw him, and a gastroscopy 10 days later. He has come back today for the results. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask these questions once each while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "So it's definitely not my heart?"
  • "Do I really have to stop the Nurofen? My knee is terrible without it."

You are relieved to have an answer. If the candidate uses jargon such as "eradication" or "PPI" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, recorded at the practice at the first visit. Clinical details: 45-year-old man with intermittent epigastric pain; pain-free at the time of recording.

  • Rate: 72/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, regular, a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal (+40°).
  • Intervals: PR 160 ms, QRS 90 ms, QTc 410 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression; T waves upright in the expected leads. No Q waves. No voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.

Conclusion: normal ECG.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus rhythm at 72, normal axis, normal PR, QRS and QTc, no ST or T wave changes, no Q waves, no LVH.
  • For John: no evidence of ischaemia or previous infarction, and it fits a gut cause for pain that is linked to meals. A normal resting ECG recorded while he is pain-free does not exclude coronary disease.
  • What it changes: it supports reassuring him, but with a father who had an MI at 60, smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol and diabetes he needs an absolute cardiovascular risk assessment. Advise him to call 000 for chest pain that is severe, getting worse or lasting more than 10 minutes, or comes with sweating, breathlessness or nausea, and to see the GP the same day for exertional chest tightness that settles with rest.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: haemoglobin 148 and MCV 88 are normal; white cells and platelets normal. Electrolytes, urea and creatinine normal. Bilirubin, ALT, AST, GGT, ALP and albumin normal. Lipase normal.
  • For John: no anaemia, so no sign of chronic blood loss or an alarm feature; normal LFTs and lipase argue against biliary disease, hepatitis and pancreatitis.
  • What it changes: normal renal function is a useful baseline, because NSAIDs with an ACE inhibitor can harm the kidneys and raise blood pressure, which is another reason to stop the ibuprofen.

handover.label: Gastroscopy and biopsy report
handover.result:
Procedure: gastroscopy (oesophagogastroduodenoscopy) under sedation, 10 days after the first visit.

Clinical details: 45-year-old man with 3 weeks of intermittent burning epigastric pain, nocturnal pain, long-term ibuprofen use. Not taking a PPI.

Findings:

  • Oesophagus: normal mucosa. No oesophagitis, no Barrett's oesophagus, no stricture or mass. Z-line regular.
  • Stomach: mild patchy erythema in the antrum. No gastric ulcer, erosions with bleeding, or mass. Normal retroflexed view.
  • Duodenum: a single 8 mm round ulcer on the anterior wall of the duodenal bulb with a clean white fibrin base. No visible vessel, adherent clot or active bleeding. Second part of the duodenum normal.

Biopsies: gastric antrum and body for H. pylori.

  • Rapid urease (CLO) test: positive.
  • Histology: chronic active gastritis with Helicobacter-like organisms seen in the antrum and body. No intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia or malignancy.

Conclusion: clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer with no stigmata of recent haemorrhage. Helicobacter pylori-associated antral gastritis.
handover.model:
• Read: normal oesophagus (no oesophagitis), mild antral gastritis, no gastric ulcer or mass, and an 8 mm clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer with no visible vessel or clot. Positive rapid urease test and H. pylori on histology, with no metaplasia, dysplasia or malignancy.
  • For John: an uncomplicated H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer, with long-term ibuprofen and smoking contributing. The duodenal site fits pain 2 to 3 hours after meals that wakes him at night. A clean base means a low risk of rebleeding, and there is no sign of cancer.
  • What it changes: he needs H. pylori eradication therapy, the ibuprofen stopped, a PPI to heal the ulcer, and a urea breath test to confirm eradication. A duodenal ulcer does not usually need a repeat scope; a gastric ulcer would.

ask: You are now handing John over to your supervising GP by phone. Please give an ISBAR handover of John Peters, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of John now, here in general practice.
Before John goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, GP; John Peters, 45, accountant.
  • Situation: 3 weeks of burning epigastric pain; gastroscopy shows an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer.
  • Background: pain 2 to 3 hours after large meals, wakes him at night, eased by antacids; no ALARM features. Ibuprofen most days for over 10 years, smokes 10 a day. Hypertension, high cholesterol, diet-controlled T2DM, knee OA. Father MI at 60.
  • Assessment: normal ECG; Hb 148, normal LFTs, lipase and renal function; 8 mm clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer, no stigmata of bleeding; CLO and histology positive for H. pylori, no dysplasia or malignancy.
  • Recommendation: 14 days of triple therapy, stop ibuprofen, PPI to heal, urea breath test to confirm eradication, smoking cessation and a cardiovascular risk assessment.

Most likely: peptic ulcer disease: a duodenal ulcer caused by H. pylori, with long-term NSAID use and smoking contributing. Burning epigastric pain 2 to 3 hours after meals, waking him at night, eased by antacids; ulcer and H. pylori on gastroscopy and biopsy.

  • GORD: burning pain eased by antacids; against: no heartburn or regurgitation, normal oesophagus.
  • Biliary colic: pain after large fatty meals, BMI 27; against: burning, no right upper quadrant or shoulder pain, Murphy's negative, normal LFTs.
  • Cardiac ischaemia: strong risk factors and father's MI at 60; against: linked to meals not exertion, normal ECG.
  • Gastric cancer: reduced appetite, H. pylori; against: age 45, no ALARM features, normal Hb, no mass, benign biopsies.

1. Explain the ulcer and the H. pylori infection in plain words, and answer his heart question honestly.
  2. Eradication therapy for 14 days: PPI (for example esomeprazole 20 mg) plus amoxicillin 1 g plus clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily. Check that he has no penicillin allergy, and warn him about diarrhoea and taste disturbance. Withhold atorvastatin during the clarithromycin course.
  3. Stop ibuprofen. For the knee: paracetamol, a topical NSAID, exercise and weight loss. If an oral NSAID is ever unavoidable, give it with a PPI.
  4. Continue the PPI once daily for about 4 more weeks after the antibiotics to heal the ulcer (NSAID-associated), then stop it at least 2 weeks before the urea breath test; Mylanta as needed.
  5. Confirm eradication with a urea breath test at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics, with the PPI stopped for 2 weeks before.
  6. Lifestyle: smoking cessation support (Quitline, pharmacotherapy).

• Call 000 or go to the ED if he vomits blood or coffee-ground material, passes black tarry or bloody stools, feels faint or collapses, or has sudden severe tummy pain.
  • Call 000 for chest pain or tightness that is severe, getting worse or lasting more than 10 minutes, or comes with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. See the GP the same day for chest tightness on exertion that settles with rest.
  • See the GP sooner if the pain does not settle, or if he has trouble swallowing, loses weight or keeps vomiting.
  • Follow-up: GP review after the 14-day course (symptoms, side effects, restart atorvastatin, knee pain plan), urea breath test at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics, cardiovascular risk assessment, quit support. Offer written information.

ddx.dx: Duodenal ulcer associated with Helicobacter pylori, with long-term NSAID use contributing
ddx.for: Burning epigastric pain 2 to 3 hours after large meals that wakes him at night, ibuprofen most days for over 10 years, a smoker, and an 8 mm duodenal bulb ulcer with H. pylori on biopsy.
Burning upper abdominal pain eased by antacids, BMI 27, spicy and fatty food.
ddx.against: No heartburn rising into the chest, regurgitation or sour taste, and a normal oesophagus at gastroscopy.
An ulcer was found at gastroscopy, so the dyspepsia is not functional.

ddx.for: Episodes of upper abdominal pain lasting 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, and fatty food with a BMI of 27.
ddx.against: Burning rather than colicky pain, no right upper quadrant or shoulder radiation, Murphy's sign negative and normal LFTs.

ddx.dx: Myocardial ischaemia presenting as epigastric pain
ddx.for: Father had an MI at 60, and he smokes and has hypertension, high cholesterol and diabetes.
ddx.against: Pain linked to meals rather than exertion, no breathlessness or sweating, and a normal ECG.

ddx.for: Mildly reduced appetite and H. pylori infection.
ddx.against: Aged 45 with no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or bleeding, a normal haemoglobin, no gastric mass and biopsies without dysplasia or malignancy.

guide:
There is no observation chart in this GP station: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The examination is normal apart from a BMI of 27. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say they will be discussed in Part 2. Whatever the candidate planned, the ECG and bloods were done on the day and the gastroscopy was arranged. In Part 2 hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. John asks his two questions once each during the management answer.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain, picks up the timing after meals and the waking at night, screens systematically for ALARM symptoms and for cardiac causes (his main worry), finds the long-term ibuprofen, smoking and stress, and examines for pallor, Virchow's node and abdominal signs. In Part 2 they read the normal ECG with appropriate caution, recognise an uncomplicated H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer, prescribe triple therapy with correct doses, stop the NSAID and offer alternatives for his knee, plan a urea breath test at the right time, notice the clarithromycin and atorvastatin interaction, and give specific bleeding, perforation and chest pain red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic abdominal pain history without ALARM symptoms or NSAIDs, dismisses or ignores his heart worry, gives a PPI alone without eradication, leaves him on ibuprofen, or does not plan to confirm eradication. Accept any PPI at the standard twice-daily eradication dose, and the regimen must be given for 14 days.
explain:
Diagnosis

John has peptic ulcer disease: an uncomplicated duodenal ulcer caused by Helicobacter pylori, with long-term NSAID use and smoking contributing. The history suggests it: burning epigastric pain linked to meals, coming 2 to 3 hours after large meals and waking him at night, worse with spicy food and partly eased by antacids. The gastroscopy with biopsy confirms it. H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two main causes of peptic ulcer, and they add to each other's risk.

ALARM features

In upper GI symptoms, ALARM features screen for gastric malignancy and complicated ulcer disease, and decide who needs prompt endoscopy:

  • Anaemia (or symptoms of it).
  • Loss of weight.
  • Anorexia. Mild loss of appetite is common in dyspepsia; marked or progressive anorexia counts.
  • Recent onset of progressive symptoms, particularly at an older age.
  • Melaena or haematemesis, and dysphagia, odynophagia or persistent vomiting.

John has none. Without ALARM features, a younger patient can reasonably be managed with a non-invasive H. pylori test (urea breath test or faecal antigen) and stopping the NSAID. Gastroscopy is the definitive test for an ulcer; it allows biopsy for H. pylori and excludes malignancy. In John's case either approach is acceptable. Stopping the NSAID and a urea breath test or faecal antigen test would be guideline-concordant; gastroscopy was chosen because of 10 years of daily NSAID use and nocturnal pain, and it gives a definitive diagnosis.

Gastric versus duodenal ulcers

  • Gastric ulcer: pain often comes soon after eating. It is more often linked to NSAIDs as well as H. pylori. Because a gastric ulcer can be malignant, it is biopsied and a repeat gastroscopy is done after treatment to confirm healing.
  • Duodenal ulcer: pain typically comes 2 to 3 hours after food and at night, when the stomach is empty, and is often eased by food or antacids. It is mostly caused by H. pylori. An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer does not usually need a repeat scope.

Differentials that matter

  • Myocardial ischaemia can present as epigastric pain, especially in people with diabetes. John's father had an MI at 60, and John smokes and has hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and diabetes, so ask about exertional symptoms and get an ECG. A normal resting ECG does not exclude coronary disease, so his risk needs assessing in its own right.
  • Aortic dissection or aneurysm: a sudden tearing pain to the back, or a pulsatile mass.
  • GORD: heartburn and regurgitation, often worse lying flat.
  • Biliary colic, cholecystitis and cholangitis: right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, radiation to the shoulder, fever and jaundice.
  • Pancreatitis: severe pain going through to the back, with a raised lipase.
  • Hepatitis, small bowel obstruction, gastroenteritis and renal colic are excluded on the history, examination and bloods.
  • Gastric cancer: the reason to screen for ALARM features.

Interpreting the results

  • ECG: normal sinus rhythm, no ischaemic changes. This is reassuring and fits a gut cause, but it does not exclude coronary disease.
  • Bloods: no anaemia, normal LFTs and lipase, and normal renal function. Renal function matters because he takes an ACE inhibitor with an NSAID.
  • Gastroscopy: a clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer with no visible vessel or clot has a low risk of rebleeding. The normal oesophagus argues against reflux oesophagitis. Antral gastritis with a positive rapid urease test and H. pylori on histology confirms infection, and there is no metaplasia, dysplasia or malignancy.

Management (eTG Gastrointestinal: peptic ulcer disease and H. pylori infection)

  • Eradication: first-line triple therapy is a PPI (for example esomeprazole 20 mg) plus amoxicillin 1 g plus clarithromycin 500 mg, all orally twice daily, for 14 days. Check for penicillin allergy first; if there is one, eTG gives an alternative regimen. Adherence is the main determinant of success. Warn about diarrhoea and taste disturbance. Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and raises atorvastatin levels (myopathy risk), so withholding the statin for the course is a simple option.
  • Ulcer healing: because the ulcer is NSAID-associated, continue the PPI once daily for about 4 more weeks after the antibiotics (roughly 6 to 8 weeks of PPI in total) to complete healing, then stop it at least 2 weeks before the urea breath test.
  • NSAIDs: stop them. For his knee osteoarthritis the RACGP guideline emphasises exercise and weight loss; paracetamol and topical NSAIDs are options. If an oral NSAID is unavoidable, use the lowest dose for the shortest time with PPI cover.
  • Confirm eradication: with a urea breath test at least 4 weeks after finishing the antibiotics, with PPIs stopped for at least 2 weeks before the test to avoid a false negative. If it is still positive, use a second-line regimen as eTG advises.
  • Lifestyle: smoking delays ulcer healing and increases recurrence, so offer cessation support (brief advice, Quitline, pharmacotherapy). Also cover limiting alcohol and trigger foods, stress management, exercise and weight.
  • Cardiovascular risk: address his concern properly with an absolute cardiovascular risk assessment, given his family history and risk factors.

Safety netting

The complications of peptic ulcer are bleeding and perforation. He should call 000 or go to the ED for haematemesis or coffee-ground vomit, melaena, fainting, or sudden severe abdominal pain. He should call 000 for chest pain or tightness that is severe, getting worse or lasting more than 10 minutes, or comes with sweating, breathlessness or nausea, and see the GP the same day for exertional chest tightness that settles with rest. He should see the GP sooner for persistent pain, dysphagia, weight loss or vomiting. Book a GP review after the course and the urea breath test.
points: Screen every patient with dyspepsia for ALARM features (anaemia, weight loss, anorexia, recent progressive symptoms at an older age, melaena or haematemesis, dysphagia or persistent vomiting): they decide who needs prompt endoscopy.
H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes of peptic ulcer. Ask specifically about over-the-counter NSAIDs, smoking and alcohol.

Duodenal ulcer pain typically comes 2 to 3 hours after meals and at night and is mostly due to H. pylori. Gastric ulcer pain comes soon after eating, is more often linked to NSAIDs, and needs a repeat scope to confirm healing and exclude cancer.
First-line eradication is 14 days of a PPI plus amoxicillin 1 g plus clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily. Check for penicillin allergy and drug interactions (clarithromycin with atorvastatin).
Confirm eradication with a urea breath test at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics, with the PPI stopped for 2 weeks before the test, and stop the NSAID.
Epigastric pain in a man with cardiovascular risk factors needs an ECG, and a normal ECG does not exclude coronary disease. Address the patient's worry about his heart directly.
